question: Does scripture (śruti) teach the Sāṃkhya's unconscious pradhāna as the cause of the world?

sides.position: Yes: pradhāna is established by inference and confirmed by scripture; reliable testimony teaches what inference does not reach.
arguments: Supersensibles are known by inference and, beyond that, by reliable scripture (SK 6).
Scripture too speaks of the world as pradhāna's product (SS 5.12); prakṛti is the first material cause, others being products per scripture (SS 6.32).
The sophist who conflicts with scripture does not attain the self (SS 6.34); Kapila recalled the Veda from the previous eon (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Sāṃkhya readings of the Kaṭha's 'unmanifest' (3.11) and the Śvetāśvatara's 'unborn one' (4.5) as prakṛti are known from the Vedānta opponent's statement of them (BS 1.4.1, 1.4.8).

sides.position: No: the scriptural cause 'saw' (reflected) before creating, so the unconscious pradhāna is not scriptural; the passages cited for Sāṃkhya mean something else, and Kapila's smṛti yields where it conflicts with śruti.
arguments: BS 1.1.5: because of 'seeing', pradhāna is non-scriptural (ChU 6.2.3 'it saw: may I be many').
BS 1.4.1: the 'unmanifest' of the Kaṭha is taken from the simile of the body (chariot image).
BS 1.4.11: the 'five fives' (BĀU 4.4.17) do not teach the twenty-five principles.
BS 2.1.1–3: rejecting Kapila's smṛti where it conflicts is no fault, since the other interpretation would leave other smṛtis without scope; the same refutes Yoga.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each side holds the other's reading of the same scriptures to be wrong.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Sāṃkhya enumerates principles analytically to discriminate self from non-self, while the Brahma Sūtra asks what the Upaniṣads teach as the conscious first cause — answers to different questions (rejected by both: Śaṅkara denies pradhāna is scriptural; classical Sāṃkhya denies any conscious director).
P4-stage: Advaita accepts the discrimination of self from the non-self as preparatory while rejecting an independent pradhāna.
Theistic Sāṃkhya synthesis (Vijñānabhikṣu, recalled): prakṛti as material cause under the Lord taught by śruti.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Śaṅkara treats Sāṃkhya as the chief opponent whose refutation refutes the others (on the last sūtra of BS 1.4) and does not accept it as a partial Vedānta; classical Sāṃkhya rejects a conscious creator (SS 5.2–12).

question: Can an unconscious pradhāna, without a conscious director, bring forth and order the world?

sides.position: Yes: prakṛti acts spontaneously for puruṣa's purpose; no Lord is needed or established.
arguments: As unconscious milk flows for the calf, pradhāna acts for puruṣa's liberation (SK 57); as people act to satisfy a longing (SK 58).

The conjunction of the seeing and the moving is like that of the lame and the blind (SK 21); the subtle body acts like an actor for puruṣa's purpose (SK 42); the instruments are made to act by no one (SK 31).
Pradhāna's activity is like milk, spontaneous like a servant's, drawn on by beginningless karma (SS 3.58–63); governance by mere proximity, like a magnet (SS 1.96).
Īśvara is not established (SS 1.92–99; 5.2–12); effects depend on ahaṃkāra, not Īśvara (SS 6.64); the attributeless cannot produce what has guṇas (Gauḍapāda on SK 61).

sides.position: No: the inferred pradhāna cannot be the cause, because an unconscious cause cannot produce orderly arrangement or activity.
arguments: Orderly arrangement is impossible for the inferred cause (BS 2.2.1), and activity too (2.2.2).
Milk and water flow under a conscious being's direction (2.2.3).
The lame-and-blind or magnet analogies fail (2.2.7); the guṇas in equilibrium cannot become principal and subordinate (2.2.8); the doctrine is incoherent (2.2.10).

sides.position: No: effects such as the world require an intelligent maker (Īśvara) as their efficient cause.
arguments: Udayana's arguments for a world-knowing, imperishable maker from effects, arrangement, support and other marks (Nyāyakusumāñjali 5.1).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether a conscious agent is required is the point at issue.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint (causal): prakṛti as material cause and a Lord as efficient cause — the theistic-Sāṃkhya reading; rejected by classical Sāṃkhya (SS 1.92) and by Advaita, for which Brahman is both material and efficient cause.
P2-standpoint (purpose): Sāṃkhya's teleology 'for puruṣa' already locates the orienting factor in consciousness (puruṣa's presence), which Vedānta places in the Lord.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Sāṃkhya denies that any Īśvara is established; Vedānta and Nyāya deny that the milk and lame-blind analogies apply without a conscious director.

question: Does a single, unconscious primal matter (pradhāna) exist as the material cause of the manifold world?

sides.position: Yes: the unmanifest is inferred from its effects, which pre-exist in it.
arguments: Prakṛti is unperceived through subtlety, not non-existence; it is known from effects (SK 8).
Because particulars are limited, homogeneous (pleasure, pain, delusion), active through potency, distinguished as cause and effect and merge back, an unmanifest cause exists (SK 14–16).
The rootless root (SS 1.67); both prakṛti and puruṣa are established by inference from general correlation (SS 1.103). Momentariness, mere consciousness and emptiness are rejected (SS 1.34–47).

sides.position: No: a single permanent cause cannot produce successive, momentary effects; the arguments from homogeneity and pre-existence fail.
arguments: Śāntarakṣita's examination of prakṛti (Tattvasaṅgraha, first chapter, with Kamalaśīla's commentary) and Bhāviveka's chapter on Sāṃkhya (Madhyamakahṛdaya 6) argue against pradhāna and satkārya (content recalled; to be extracted from their texts).

historical_debates.name: Vindhyavāsa against Buddhamitra
historical_debates.accounts: Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu: the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa defeated Vasubandhu's teacher Buddhamitra in debate before a king at Ayodhyā and was rewarded; Vasubandhu replied with a (lost) Paramārthasaptati refuting Sāṃkhya.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Buddhist account: Buddhamitra lost, Vasubandhu later refuted the Sāṃkhya text; no Sāṃkhya account known.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: permanence and momentariness are both insisted upon.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: substance (dravyārthika) vs mode (paryāyārthika) — enduring prakṛti vs changing modifications; both traditions reject this: Sāṃkhya holds the modifications real transformations of one substance, Buddhists deny any enduring substrate.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Buddhist pramāṇa authors deny any permanent substance; Sāṃkhya calls the emptiness view 'mere slander by the unawakened' (SS 1.45).

question: Is the conscious self one or many?

sides.position: Many: each being has its own puruṣa.
arguments: Birth, death and the instruments are allotted separately; beings do not act all at once; the guṇas differ (SK 18; SS 1.149, 6.45).
Vāmadeva and others were liberated while others were not (SS 1.157).
If distribution is by adjuncts, duality returns once they are established (SS 6.46); difference is known from marks (SS 5.61).

sides.position: One: the self is one; apparent plurality comes from limiting adjuncts, like space in pots.
arguments: The self appears as individual selves like space as pot-spaces (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.3–9); this is the objection the Sāṃkhya Sūtra itself states (1.150).

reconciliation.explanation: Sāṃkhya's own reading (SS 1.154): non-duality texts speak of sameness of kind, plurality of number — one and many under different standpoints.
reconciliation.detail: Under P2, 'one' names the single nature (pure consciousness) all puruṣas share and 'many' the number of seers; this is how the Sāṃkhya Sūtra reconciles scripture with plurality. It does not claim numerical identity.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advaita rejects the reading: the texts of non-duality teach numerical identity of the self with Brahman, and plurality belongs to adjuncts.

question: Does killing prescribed in Vedic sacrifice incur demerit?

sides.position: Yes, slightly: the Vedic means are impure because of the killing; the general prohibition of harm still applies.
arguments: The Vedic means are bound up with impurity (SK 2), explained as the killing of animals (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati).
Pañcaśikha: 'a slight admixture, removable, bearable' — the demerit is small and expiable.
The prohibition 'do not harm any being' and the injunction to offer the animal have different objects: one makes known harm to the agent, the other service to the sacrifice (Vācaspati).

sides.position: No: killing enjoined by the Veda for the sacrifice is dharma; the specific injunction prevails over the general prohibition.
arguments: As stated by the opponent in the Tattvakaumudī on SK 2: the general rule 'do not harm' is set aside by the specific injunction to offer the animal to Agni-Soma.
Mīmāṃsā's own discussion (Śabara on MS 1.1.2, the śyena rite) is recalled here, not checked.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether any demerit remains is the point at issue.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: ritual standpoint (the act fulfils the sacrifice and is dharma) vs ethical-karmic standpoint (the act harms a being and leaves a trace of adharma) — Vācaspati's own 'different objects' argument; Mīmāṃsā denies the second.
P4-stage: Mīmāṃsā addresses those qualified for heaven-bringing rites; Sāṃkhya those seeking final release.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mīmāṃsā holds that enjoined killing produces no demerit.

question: Are the sense and action capacities made of the elements, or products of ahaṃkāra?

sides.position: Products of ahaṃkāra (classical Sāṃkhya).
arguments: The eleven organs proceed from ahaṃkāra in its sāttvika aspect (SK 25).
They are not elemental, since scripture speaks of them as from ahaṃkāra (SS 2.20, 5.84).

sides.position: Elemental: the senses come from the elements.
arguments: Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.12: smell, taste, sight, touch and hearing are the senses, from the elements.

sides.position: Elemental, per the Sāṃkhya teacher Pañcādhikaraṇa (a dissenting Sāṃkhya view).
arguments: The Yuktidīpikā on SK 22 reports that for Pañcādhikaraṇa the organs are elemental (bhautika).

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: constitution (Nyāya: what the organ is made of) vs function (Sāṃkhya: the organ as instrument of the I-sense).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Sāṃkhya explicitly denies elemental organs (SS 5.84).

question: Are the instruments thirteen or eleven? (a debate among Sāṃkhya teachers)

sides.position: Thirteen: buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and ten external capacities, each inner organ with its own function (classical).
arguments: SK 29, 32–33; functions distinct (SK 23, 24, 27).

sides.position: Eleven: the functions of construction, self-assertion and determination are one; all objects are apprehended in manas (Vindhyavāsin).
arguments: Reported by the Yuktidīpikā on SK 22.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: a counting convention — one inner organ with three functions vs three organs.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kārikā tradition keeps thirteen as its teaching.

question: Is there a subtle body that transmigrates? (a debate among Sāṃkhya teachers)

sides.position: Yes: a constant subtle body transmigrates, perfumed by the dispositions (classical; Pañcādhikaraṇa's permanent conveying body; Patañjali's successive subtle bodies).
arguments: SK 39–42; Yuktidīpikā on SK 39 for the variants.

sides.position: No: since the organs are all-pervading, birth is their functioning at the seed-place and death its abandonment (Vindhyavāsin).
arguments: Yuktidīpikā on SK 39; Kumārila reports that Vindhyavāsin did not accept an intermediate body (recalled).

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: whether the vehicle of rebirth is conceived as a body or as the functioning of pervasive organs.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kārikā tradition teaches the subtle body (SK 40).

question: Is there one prakṛti for all puruṣas, or one for each? (a debate among Sāṃkhya teachers)

sides.position: One prakṛti, common to all (classical).
arguments: The manifest and pradhāna are common (SK 11); there is only one prakṛti, cause of the three worlds (Gauḍapāda on SK 66); no means of knowledge establishes many (Yuktidīpikā on SK 56).

sides.position: A separate pradhāna for each puruṣa, all following the pradhāna of the great-bodied one (Paurika).
arguments: Reported by the Yuktidīpikā on SK 56.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: cosmic prakṛti (one) vs individual prakṛti as each puruṣa's field of experience (many).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Yuktidīpikā rejects Paurika's view for want of proof.

question: What causes the owner–owned relation between puruṣa and prakṛti? (views recorded in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra)

sides.position: Karma: the relation is caused by karma and is beginningless like seed and sprout (SS 6.67).
Non-discrimination (Pañcaśikha, SS 6.68).
The subtle body (the teacher Sanandana, SS 6.69).

reconciliation.explanation: The sūtra records the three as alternatives without rejecting any; they name the relation's cause at different removes (non-discrimination at the root, karma as its working, the subtle body as its carrier).
reconciliation.detail: Non-discrimination is elsewhere called the cause of the conjunction (SS 1.55) and bondage itself (SS 6.16), which supports reading the three as compatible.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: None recorded in the texts consulted.

question: Does Sāṃkhya deny Īśvara, or only deny that an eternal creator is proved?

sides.position: No Īśvara is established as creator (classical; the Sāṃkhya Sūtra; Aniruddha as recalled), though emergent lords exist.
arguments: The SK is silent; Gauḍapāda argues the attributeless Īśvara cannot produce what has guṇas (on SK 61).
'Īśvara is not established' (SS 1.92); neither free nor bound he could not create (1.93–94); fruit comes from karma (5.2); effects depend on ahaṃkāra (6.64).
Yet one absorbed in prakṛti becomes an all-knowing, all-doing lord in the next creation (SS 3.55–57).

sides.position: The denial is a concessive argument; Īśvara is known from scripture (Vijñānabhikṣu, recalled).
arguments: Vijñānabhikṣu salutes the Lord (Sāṃkhyasāra 1.1.1) and reads SS 1.92 as not denying a Lord taught in śruti (recalled, low confidence).

sides.position: A Lord as twenty-sixth principle above the twenty-five (epic Sāṃkhya).
arguments: Mokṣadharma dialogues (e.g., Vasiṣṭha and Karāla Janaka) — recalled, U05 to confirm.

candidate_readings: P5-neyartha: Vijñānabhikṣu's own reading — the denial is provisional (for argument's sake), the scriptural Lord definitive; classical commentators take the denial at face value.
P4-stage: denial of an eternal Lord to cut attachment to lordship in aspirants (recalled as Vijñānabhikṣu's explanation; verify).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Sāṃkhya (Gauḍapāda; the sūtras' own arguments) rejects a creator Lord.

notes: U50 owns dsp:isvara; this entry records the question within Sāṃkhya.

question: What appears in erroneous cognition? (theories of error)

sides.position: The existent-and-non-existent (sadasatkhyāti): the erroneous object is sublated as there and not sublated as real elsewhere.
arguments: Error is not the appearance of the non-existent, nor of the existent, nor of the indescribable, nor appearance-as-other (SS 5.52–55); it is sadasatkhyāti (5.56).

sides.position: The indescribable (anirvacanīyakhyāti): the erroneous object is neither real nor unreal.
arguments: The Sāṃkhya Sūtra rejects this view (5.54); Advaita's own texts to be cited by U13.

sides.position: Appearance-as-other (anyathākhyāti): a real thing elsewhere appears as something it is not.
arguments: The Sāṃkhya Sūtra rejects this view (5.55); Nyāya's own texts to be cited by U11.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: each theory describes error from a different ontological standpoint (realist, indeterminist, relocation).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school rejects the others' accounts (SS 5.52–55).

sides.position: Isolation (kaivalya): the complete cessation of the threefold suffering; puruṣa has no properties, so liberation is not bliss, motion, annihilation or powers.
arguments: SK 68; SS 1.1, 3.85; liberation is only the destruction of obstacles (SS 6.20); not the manifestation of bliss, destruction of specific qualities, going to a place, total destruction, emptiness, gaining powers or Indra's rank (SS 5.74–83); the praise of liberation as bliss is for the dull (SS 5.68).

sides.position: Liberation is realizing one's nature as Brahman, which is bliss.
arguments: Advaita texts to be cited by U13 (e.g., Taittirīya Up. on Brahman as bliss).

sides.position: Liberation is absolute release from pain (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.22), with the cessation of the self's specific qualities (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika).
arguments: Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.22 (recalled).

sides.position: The liberated soul rises to the summit of the world (Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.5, recalled).
arguments: Rejected by SS 5.76: the inactive does not go anywhere.

candidate_readings: P1-level / P2-standpoint: descriptions by negation (Sāṃkhya, Nyāya: cessation of suffering) vs by affirmation (Advaita: bliss) of a state all agree is beyond saṃsāra.
P7-arthavāda: Sāṃkhya itself reads 'bliss' as figurative praise (SS 5.67–68).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sāṃkhya denies that puruṣa has bliss as a property; Advaita holds bliss is Brahman's nature, not a property.

question: Is consciousness a product of the combined elements of the body?

sides.position: No: consciousness is not found in the elements separately, nor in combination; puruṣa, other than the body, exists.
arguments: SS 3.20–22, 5.129, 6.1–3; SK 17 (aggregates exist for another).

sides.position: Yes: consciousness arises from the combination of elements, as intoxicating power from ingredients.
arguments: Stated as the opponent's view in SS 3.22; Cārvāka's own sūtras survive only in quotations.

candidate_readings: P1-level: the materialist account as a description of embodied consciousness only (rejected by both).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sāṃkhya holds puruṣa distinct from all elements; Cārvāka denies any self beyond the body.

sides.position: No: recognition shows persistence; momentary things could not stand in causal relation.
arguments: SS 1.34–41; mere-consciousness and emptiness views also rejected (1.42–47).

sides.position: Yes: whatever exists is momentary (the Buddhist pramāṇa school).
arguments: Dharmakīrti's and Śāntarakṣita's arguments for momentariness (to be cited by U41).

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: substance vs mode (as in dsp:existence-of-pradhana).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Both sides reject a standpoint reading.
